posts.cooked:
Hey everyone!

I’m a small business owner here in Austin, and I’m wondering if anyone else is drowning in spreadsheet chaos like I am.

When I first started out, Excel felt like my best friend - simple, straightforward, got the job done. But as things have grown, I’m running into some real headaches that are honestly keeping me up at night:

  • My inventory counts keep coming up wrong (and I have no idea where the disconnect is happening)

  • I’ve got cash tied up in products that just aren’t moving

  • Somehow I keep missing when popular items go out of stock

I know I’m not the only one dealing with this stuff, so I’m curious - what’s the one spreadsheet struggle that makes you want to pull your hair out the most? Is it trying to forecast what you’ll actually need? Keeping track of inventory counts? Managing purchase orders? Updating product listings? Or maybe something completely different that I haven’t even thought of yet?

And if you’ve found anything that actually works - whether it’s a template that saved your sanity, a workflow that clicked, an app that was worth the money, or even just a clever little script - I’d love to hear about it.

I’m planning to put together a helpful roundup from whatever tips come out of this conversation, so thanks in advance for sharing your wisdom! We’re all in this together

Tag: inventory, forecasting, purchase orders, spreadsheets, excel, ops

If you ever expand to managing multiple Shopify stores, you might want to look at Tipo Multistore Inventory Sync – it keeps inventory perfectly in sync across all stores so you don’t have to juggle spreadsheets.

For a single-store setup though, tools like Stocky by Shopify or Inventory Planner may be more practical for forecasting, low-stock alerts, and purchase order tracking.

Oh I feel this one. I started out tracking everything in spreadsheets too — they work great until you realize you’re spending half your week chasing mismatched numbers.

For me, the worst part was realizing I had products going out of stock without noticing. That’s what finally pushed me to build a tiny tool called Elevix: Low Stock Alert — it just emails you once a day with a quick list of anything running low, so you can reorder before it becomes a problem.

It’s been a sanity saver for me and a few other small stores. Totally agree though — spreadsheets are amazing until they quietly turn into your biggest risk!

If your inventory counts are wrong then no app can help with that. Sounds like it could be an issue in your warehouse or similar, but obv I don’t know.

If some products or product categories aren’t moving, you can check Portfolytics, use it 60 days for free, and then cancel it

For out of stock products, there should be plenty of apps to warn you when they are about to be sold out?

My number one enemy when I was still an ecom manager was probably product data that just took about third of my time even though we only had about 1000 products.. We eventually bought a fancy system to manage it all.

posts.cooked:
I do this cleanup for sellers for a living and the pattern is almost always identical: the spreadsheet was fine at 50 SKUs and broke at 500 because stock and history were mixed in one place. Worth trying the split before paying for software — if it doesn’t fix it, you’ll at least know the problem was process, not the tool.Cash tied up in slow movers: SUMIFS on Movements by SKU over the last 90 days, then sort ascending. Anything with stock on hand but no movement is your dead capital, and now you can see it as a number instead of a feeling.Low stock alert: conditional formatting on the Stock tab, highlight the row where the calculated quantity is below the reorder point pulled from Products with VLOOKUP.Two things fall out of this almost for free:From then on the on-hand figure is calculated, so it can’t drift. When a physical count disagrees, you append a “recount” row with the difference instead of typing over the old value — and you keep the audit trail, which is the part that actually tells you where the disconnect happened.Stock: SKU in column A, and in column B a formula instead of a typed number:

=SUMIFS(Movements!C:C,Movements!B:B,A2)-SUMIFS(Movements!D:D,Movements!B:B,A2)Movements: date, SKU, qty in, qty out, reason (sale / return / damage / recount). Append-only — you never overwrite a row here.Products: SKU, name, cost, reorder point. One row per SKU, rarely edited.The fix is boring but it works, and it costs nothing. Split one sheet into three tabs:Before you buy another app — the reason counts keep coming up wrong is usually not Excel. It’s that the sheet is doing two jobs at once: it holds the current stock number AND the history of how it changed. Once those live in the same column, every manual edit silently breaks the count, and nothing downstream can be trusted.

One thing that helps: stop keeping everything in one sheet. Keep one “master” sheet that mirrors your Shopify columns exactly (same order, never changed), and keep each supplier’s file separate in their own format. You only ever copy from supplier sheet to master sheet, so when counts go wrong you can trace which import caused it.

A simple change-log tab (date, file, rows added/changed) also saves hours of detective work later.

ai_summary.summarized_text:
A small business owner describes inventory errors, cash tied up in slow-moving products, and missed restocking opportunities as spreadsheets become harder to manage with business growth. Replies suggest that the main pain points vary: stock accuracy, low-stock alerts, forecasting, and product-data maintenance.

The most detailed recommendation is to separate a workbook into three tabs: a product reference list, an append-only movements log for sales, returns, damage, and recounts, and a stock view that calculates current quantities from the log. This preserves an audit trail and helps identify discrepancies. Other process tips include using a 90-day movement calculation to flag slow sellers, conditional formatting for reorder thresholds, and keeping supplier files separate from a consistent master sheet with a change log.

Several commenters recommend Shopify inventory, forecasting, alert, or product-information apps; these are suggestions rather than agreed solutions. One reply cautions that software cannot correct inaccurate physical counts. No single tool or approach was selected, and the discussion remains open.
